rv.q: Her performance triumphantly walks a knife edge between virtuosity and absurdity.

Adapted and directed by Kip Williams, Australia’s most innovative theatre-maker, the project is a companion piece to his recent, triumphant The Picture of Dorian Gray, which saw Succession’s multitasking Sarah Snook bag an Olivier and a Tony.
If the production falters, it's for reasons largely extraneous to her.

One where the standing ovation at the end is, yes, absolutely for her from Wicked, her from Harriet, Oscar-nominated for both, the south Londoner who did fine at home but became a star once she went to the US. Yet the 39-year-old’s first British theatre show in more than a decade too often feels like eavesdropping on the making of her latest film.
It's sad that the production plays so little to Erivo's strengths, which might better have been reconceived as Dracula the Musical.

The overall effect is slightly ramshackle, sluggish and, in the end, frustratingly short on dash and drama.Continues... Erivo, simply dressed in a singlet and trousers, lies flat on the stage; above her, a giant screen that creates the impression of a sleepless night.
In a virtuoso press night performance she slayed doubters like a vampire hunter administering a stake to the heart.
...it appears that the blood really has been drained from this production, leaving everything in colourless tones and cast in Nick Schlieper’s sickly white light.
It is not her failure that the only performer on stage for an hour and 50 minutes should feel strangely underemployed.

Since the release of Wicked in 2024 and its sequel last year, the actress, 39, and her co-star Ariana Grande, 32, have been lambasted with criticism over their behaviour during the promo bliz. Cynthia, who starred as Elphaba, and Ariana, as Glinda, were snubbed of an Oscar nomination this season despite the rave reviews the movie has received.
The triumphant Snook in The Picture of Dorian Gray was runner up for my play of the year in 2024; Erivo and Dracula will not be achieving such a position this time around.
Erivo deserves it, but she also deserves far better – a Dracula with a bit of red meat rather than this bloodless, soul-sapping affair.
Alas, this time it feels effortful rather than fluent – and Erivo seems too stressed to offer more than the odd glimpse of Dracula’s coolly gothic allure.

In one version, the task disappears and the road trip continues; in the other, the labour itself becomes the spectacle. That has always been my hesitation with one-person shows. However impressive the feat, the sheer scale of the exertion can eclipse the narrative you came to see.
The show is a mesmerising sight.

Others found the format overwhelming and ineffective, with the screens distracting, and the approach not making full use of Cynthia Erivo's talents. Across the board, it was universally agreed that Erivo delivered a captivating and compelling performance.

The production is a technical feat, but is so caught up in its own cleverness that it forgets one of the most intrinsic appeals of theatre; to connect an actor to an audience through their live presence on stage.
This is, regrettably, one of the worst evenings I have spent in a West End theatre.
Watching TV in the theatre is like visiting a restaurant to read the menu.
